videoAnalyses.title: Alexis Hawes Health Everyday Health Hacks - Alexis Hawes
videoAnalyses.summary: Alexis Hawes, a board-certified health and wellness coach, shares ten simple, everyday health hacks to optimize well-being and promote longevity. These practical tips range from walking after meals and using glass water bottles to optimizing sleep and practicing portion control, demonstrating that improving health doesn't have to be overly complex.
videoAnalyses.fullTranscript:
I'm Alexis Hawes, Founder of Alexis Hawes Health and a National Board Certified Health and Wellness Coach. I couldn't be more excited to be here with you today on Jet Sweat.

This week, we're diving into simple health hacks. It's a common misconception that we have to make our health overly complex and difficult. Today, I'll dive into some of these top tips and share some of the practical things that I've incorporated, as well as my clients, into their everyday lives.

The first is walking after meals. Walking even 10 to 15 minutes can help lower your blood sugar spikes and improve digestion. Next is using reusable glass water bottles at home. Many Americans consume all of their water through bottled water sources. Studies are now showing if you consume water in this way, you could be ingesting up to a credit card worth of plastic each and every week. Installing a water filter under your sink and using glass water bottles at home can help avoid the harmful chemicals found in plastic that often disrupt hormone function.

When it comes to our eye health, we can follow a 20-20-20 rule. If you're looking at a screen for 20 minutes, then stare off 20 feet away for 20 seconds. This can significantly improve eye strain throughout your day. This next healthy habit is not for everyone, especially those who hate cold showers, but taking a cold shower even for a minute or two has been shown to have huge improvements to our health, including supporting the immune system, stimulating blood flow, and creating mental clarity.

When it comes to our morning routines and optimizing our circadian rhythm, it's hugely important to get first light. The light that's shining bright and early, first thing in the morning. Studies are now showing that consuming one tablespoon of apple cider vinegar or white vinegar diluted in a glass of water before you eat can have a significant impact on your blood sugar spikes. It can also help aid digestion and therefore support insulin resistance.

When it comes to our teeth health, there's a healthy hack of oil pulling. Taking just a small scoop of coconut oil, putting it in your mouth and swishing it around can support oral health by reducing bacteria and freshening your breath. Optimizing your sleep routine, doing things like avoiding screens late at night, using blackout curtains, and even mouth tape has been shown in studies to promote and optimize our sleep patterns. As it relates to portion control, opting for a smaller plate can help you eat less by tricking your brain into feeling satisfied with smaller portions.

To improve circulation, promote relaxation, and reduce swelling, you can lay on your bed and simply raise your feet on the wall. Even doing this for just a few minutes can have a huge impact. These are just a handful of ways that we can biohack our routines to optimize our health, promote longevity, and reduce our risks for chronic disease. I would love to hear how you begin incorporating these simple habits into your daily routines, and if I missed anything that's been working for you, don't hesitate to share. Be sure to check back in to week 39 where I'll be delivering your fourth and final seasonal recipe guide of the year. Until then, start trying these healthy hacks and I'll see you soon.

videoAnalyses.title: Alexis Hawes Health Macronutrients - Alexis Hawes
videoAnalyses.summary: Alexis Hawes breaks down the three essential macronutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, explaining their vital roles in the body. She debunks common diet culture myths, emphasizing the importance of whole foods and quality over quantity. Ultimately, she highlights that nutrition is highly personal and should be approached with bio-individuality in mind.
videoAnalyses.fullTranscript:
I'm Alexis Hawes, founder of Alexis Hawes Health and a National Board Certified Health and Wellness Coach. I couldn't be more excited to be here with you today on Jet Sweat.

This week we're diving into macronutrients. Macronutrients are the three nutrients that our body needs in large amounts to function properly. They include carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, and they help with bodily processes like metabolism, our hormones, and muscle growth.

Now there's a lot of misinformation when it comes to macronutrients, especially as it relates to weight loss. For example, carbohydrates are often demonized, even though they are our body's preferred source of energy. Particularly, they are crucial for our brain health. But it's important to know that there's two main types of carbs. Simple carbohydrates are digested rapidly and are a quick source of energy. They show up as sugars in things like fruit, while complex carbohydrates take longer to digest and are a more sustainable source of energy, and they're found in things like whole grains and vegetables. When it comes to weight management and living a healthy lifestyle, you want to focus on whole fruits, whole vegetables, and whole grains. Where we get into trouble is when we have refined the carbohydrates, when we've milled down the wheat to make white flour that's processed, or we turn whole fruits into fruit juices that can easily spike our blood sugar levels. Focusing on whole foods will enrich your fiber intake, slow down your digestion, and prevent blood sugar spikes.

The next macronutrient is protein. We have seen so much marketing around protein, but did you know that the average American eats twice the amount of protein they need and only half the amount of fiber? Protein is essential for repairing tissue, building muscle, and balancing hormones, but it's a common misconception that it can only be found in animal foods. The reality is is there's a vast amount of protein in plant-based foods as well. Things like nuts, beans, legumes, and even vegetables and leafy greens.

And the third and final macronutrient that is crucial for our body's health are fats. Again, this has been something that is often demonized in weight loss culture. There was a huge epidemic of having low-fat foods because at one point our society thought they were healthier. Fats are essential though for absorbing fat-soluble vitamins such as A, D, E, and K. They also help with brain health and hormone regulation. Similar to carbohydrates and proteins, there are fats that are healthier and less healthy for you. Unsaturated fats help promote health and reduce inflammation. Things like avocado, extra virgin olive oil, nuts, and fish. Meanwhile, saturated and trans fats found in processed food and fried food can increase cholesterol levels and lead to heart disease. When it comes to all three of these macronutrients, it's important to focus on quality versus quantity. The majority of Americans are overloading their protein intake and not getting enough carbohydrates.

When it comes to our dietary behaviors, it's important to consider things like your physical activity level, genetics, access to food, and your personal health goals. There is no one-size-fits-all, but each and every one of us should look at our food as bio-individual.

curriculum.targetTransformation: Rewire your brain. Stop fighting yourself.

lessons.title: Add two effortless habits to your day that lower blood sugar and protect your body
lessons.summary: Learners discover that walking after meals and switching to glass water bottles are two low-effort, high-impact habits they can start immediately to reduce blood sugar spikes and avoid hormone-disrupting chemicals.

sessions.title: Two habits that start working today
sessions.summary: Alexis introduces the core premise that health doesn't have to be complex, then walks through the first two actionable hacks: post-meal walking and glass water bottle use.

steps.title: Schedule a 10-minute post-meal walk into your day today
Reflect on what 'not making health complex' actually means for your routine

clips.chapterTitle: Health doesn't have to be hard

lessons.title: Stop demonizing carbs — understand what your body actually runs on
lessons.summary: Learners cut through diet-culture noise by learning the real definition of macronutrients, why carbohydrates are the body's preferred fuel source, and the critical difference between simple and complex carbs.

sessions.title: What macronutrients actually do — and why carbs aren't the enemy
sessions.summary: Alexis defines macronutrients and their roles in metabolism, hormones, and muscle growth, then breaks down the two types of carbohydrates and why whole foods prevent the blood sugar spikes that refined carbs cause.

steps.title: Audit one day of your carbohydrate intake and label each source as simple or complex
Reflect on how the simple vs. complex carb distinction changes your view of a food you currently avoid or over-eat

clips.chapterTitle: Macronutrients defined — and why carbs are misunderstood

lessons.title: Protect your eyes, immune system, and sleep with three more daily hacks
lessons.summary: Learners add the 20-20-20 rule for eye strain, cold showers for immune and mental clarity benefits, and circadian rhythm optimization through morning sunlight exposure to their daily toolkit.

sessions.title: Three hacks for your eyes, immunity, and circadian rhythm
sessions.summary: Alexis picks up from the first health hacks segment to introduce screen-related eye strain relief, cold shower benefits, and the importance of first morning light for optimizing circadian rhythm.

steps.title: Try the 20-20-20 rule during your next screen session and log what you notice
Reflect on which of these three hacks — 20-20-20, cold shower, or morning light — your brain resists most and why

clips.chapterTitle: The 20-20-20 rule, cold showers, and morning light

lessons.title: Build a nutrition approach that fits your biology, not someone else's diet plan
lessons.summary: Learners complete their macronutrient understanding by learning the truth about protein intake, the essential roles of healthy fats, and the concept of bio-individuality — so they can design eating habits based on their own activity level, genetics, and health goals.

sessions.title: Protein, fats, and eating for your unique biology
sessions.summary: Alexis corrects the myth that Americans need more protein, reveals that the real deficit is fiber, explains the difference between unsaturated and saturated fats, and closes with the principle of bio-individuality — no one-size-fits-all nutrition.

steps.title: Write your personal bio-individual nutrition profile using Alexis's four factors
Reflect on how bio-individuality changes the way you judge your eating choices
